claim: Caenorhabditis tropicalis was identified by Marie-Anne Félix in 2008.
source: Caenorhabditis tropicalis was identified by Marie-Anne Félix in 2008 (Kiontke et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kiontke et al., 2011

claim: A comprehensive reference genome for C. tropicalis is lacking.
source: However, a comprehensive reference genome for the species is lacking and relatively little is known of its biology and ecology.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge at the time of writing

claim: C. tropicalis has a more restricted range than other selfing Caenorhabditis species.
source: Global sampling indicates a more restricted range than that of the other selfers (Félix, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Félix, 2020

claim: C. tropicalis shows extremely low levels of genetic diversity at a handful of loci.
source: the single study of C. tropicalis population genetics and reproductive compatibility found extremely low levels of genetic diversity at a handful of loci (Gimond et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gimond et al., 2013

claim: Crosses among and sometimes within C. tropicalis locales revealed outbreeding depression.
source: Crosses among, and sometimes within, locales revealed outbreeding depression, a result common to the selfers (Baird and Stonesifer, 2012; Dolgin et al., 2007; Ross et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Outbreeding depression was particularly acute in C. tropicalis, with embryonic lethality and developmentally abnormal F2 progeny common among certain hybrid crosses.
source: Outbreeding depression was particularly acute in C. tropicalis, with embryonic lethality and developmentally abnormal F2 progeny common among certain hybrid crosses (Gimond et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gimond et al., 2013

claim: Male mating ability in C. tropicalis was found to be generally poor, though highly variable.
source: Male mating ability was also found to be generally poor, though highly variable, which together with low genetic diversity suggests an especially high rate of selfing.
evidence: Inference from observations reported in the manuscript

claim: Classical models of selfing evolution predict that selfing will evolve when the reduction in reproduction due to inbreeding depression is less than one half.
source: Classical models start with the doubling of reproductive rate achieved by selfers (through the elimination of males in the case of Caenorhabditis) and note that selfing will evolve when the reduction in reproduction due to inbreeding depression is less than one half (Cutter, 2019; Goodwillie et al., 2005; Lande and Schemske, 1985; Lively and Lloyd, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical literature

claim: Selfing has benefits for reproductive assurance, allowing a single individual to colonize a new environment.
source: Selfing has benefits for reproductive assurance (Baker, 1955; Theologidis et al., 2014), allowing a single individual to colonize a new environment
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker, 1955 and Theologidis et al., 2014

claim: Selfing allows for rapid adaptation when traits are jointly determined by maternal and zygotic genotypes.
source: and it allows for rapid adaptation when traits are jointly determined by maternal and zygotic genotypes (Drown and Wade, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Drown and Wade, 2014

claim: Selfing slows adaptation to new environments or pathogens by reducing recombination and genetic diversity.
source: On the other hand, selfing slows adaptation to new environments or pathogens by reducing recombination and genetic diversity, while increasing the load of weakly deleterious mutations (Cutter, 2019; Kamran-Disfani and Agrawal, 2014; Morran et al., 2009, Morran et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: A chromosome-scale genome for C. tropicalis was assembled.
source: To study the causes and effects of mating system evolution in Caenorhabditis, we assembled a chromosome-scale genome for C. tropicalis, oriented by linkage data from recombinant inbred lines (RILs).
evidence: Direct statement of work performed in this study

claim: The population structure of a global sample of C. tropicalis isolates is very strong.
source: We show with short-read mapping against this reference that the population structure of a global sample of isolates is very strong, which is an expected side-effect of selfing.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript

claim: C. tropicalis shows extreme heterogeneity in the distribution of genetic diversity across the genome.
source: We also find extreme heterogeneity in the distribution of genetic diversity across the genome.
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript

claim: Outbreeding depression in C. tropicalis is due largely to maternal-effect haplotypes that kill offspring that do not inherit them.
source: Here, we show that it is due largely to a different process in C. tropicalis: maternal-effect haplotypes that kill offspring that do not inherit them.
evidence: Supported by genetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: Haplotypes that behave as maternal-effect killers are known as Medea elements.
source: Haplotypes that behave in this way are known as Medea elements (Beeman et al., 1992; Beeman and Friesen, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to Beeman et al., 1992 and Beeman and Friesen, 1999

claim: Medea elements represent a form of post-zygotic gene drive.
source: and they represent a form of post-zygotic gene drive (Price et al., 2020; Wade and Beeman, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Price et al., 2020 and Wade and Beeman, 1994

claim: Medea elements impose severe fitness costs on heterozygous mothers.
source: Medeas impose severe fitness costs on heterozygous mothers
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript

claim: Selfing limits the spread of Medea elements.
source: and simulations show that selfing limits their spread.
evidence: Supported by simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: Frequent selfing in C. tropicalis may be a strategy to avoid Medea-mediated outbreeding depression.
source: Frequent selfing in C. tropicalis may therefore be a strategy to avoid Medea-mediated outbreeding depression.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and simulations

claim: Wild isolates of C. tropicalis vary greatly in their propensity or ability to outcross.
source: This analysis shows that wild isolates of C. tropicalis, and males in particular, vary greatly in their propensity or ability to outcross.
evidence: Supported by mating trial data presented in Figure 1A

claim: Male crossing probability was much more variable than that of hermaphrodites in C. tropicalis.
source: Male crossing probability was much more variable than that of hermaphrodites, consistent with relaxed selection (residual deviance of 179.2 vs. 85.2, null deviance 232.6, binomial linear model) (Cutter, 2019; Jalinsky et al., 2020; Noble et al., 2015; Palopoli et al., 2008; van der Kooi and Schwander, 2014).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mating trial data and citations to relevant literature

claim: Same-strain pairings were indistinguishable from inter-strain pairings in outcrossing probability.
source: Same-strain pairings were indistinguishable from inter-strain pairings (p=0.88, likelihood ratio test [LRT] of binomial linear models).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mating trial data

claim: Two C. tropicalis strains (JU1630 and JU1373) lost males and were reproducing solely by selfing after 10 generations of passaging.
source: At the end, two strains, JU1630 and JU1373, had lost males and were reproducing solely by selfing
evidence: Supported by passaging experiment data presented in Figure 1B

claim: Three C. tropicalis strains retained males at frequencies of 20–40% after 10 generations of passaging.
source: The other strains retained males at frequencies of 20–40%.
evidence: Supported by passaging experiment data presented in Figure 1B

claim: The NIC58 nuclear genome assembly comprised 81.3 Mb in 15 sequences.
source: The resulting nuclear genome assembly comprised 81.3 Mb in 15 sequences.
evidence: Direct statement of assembly results

claim: The X chromosome of C. tropicalis NIC58 assembled as a single contig.
source: The X chromosome assembled as a single contig, and all other chromosomes were oriented genetically into pseudochromosomes.
evidence: Direct statement of assembly results

claim: The NIC58 mitochondrial genome is 13,935 bp.
source: We assembled a 13,935 bp mitochondrial genome from short-reads, followed by circular extension with long-reads.
evidence: Direct statement of assembly results

claim: The NIC58 nuclear genome contains 21,210 protein-coding genes.
source: We annotated nuclear genomes using mixed-stage short-read RNAseq data, calling 21,210 protein-coding genes for NIC58
evidence: Direct statement of annotation results

claim: The JU1373 nuclear genome contains 20,829 protein-coding genes.
source: calling 21,210 protein-coding genes for NIC58 and 20,829 for JU1373
evidence: Direct statement of annotation results

claim: C. tropicalis is widely distributed within 25° of the Equator and absent outside this region.
source: C. tropicalis is widely distributed within 25° of the Equator and absent outside this region (Félix, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Félix, 2020

claim: The genome-wide estimate of nucleotide diversity in C. tropicalis is around three times higher than previously reported.
source: Though not directly comparable, the genome-wide estimate of nucleotide diversity provided here is around three times higher (genotype set 1, median value across 20 kb windows = 0.00097)
evidence: Comparison of current data to previous study by Gimond et al., 2013

claim: Mitochondrial diversity in C. tropicalis is higher than nuclear diversity.
source: with mitochondrial diversity higher again as expected (0.0038).
evidence: Supported by data and general expectation

claim: Up to 1.3% of the NIC58-alignable fraction of the genome lacks aligned reads among any single C. tropicalis isolate.
source: Indeed, we found rampant missingness in our data; up to 1.3% of the NIC58-alignable fraction of the genome lacks aligned reads among any single isolate
evidence: Supported by analysis of sequencing data

claim: 7.8% of the alignable C. tropicalis genome lacks reads in at least one isolate.
source: and 7.8% of the alignable genome lacks reads in at least one (considering only those with >25 × mapped and paired reads, for which missing data and sequencing depth are uncorrelated, r = 0.13, p=0.65).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sequencing data

claim: C. tropicalis shows very low genetic diversity genome-wide.
source: These results establish that C. tropicalis shows very low genetic diversity genome-wide
evidence: Supported by genome-wide diversity data

claim: C. tropicalis has many regions sufficiently divergent that reference-based mapping fails.
source: but also suggest this homogeneity is broken by many regions sufficiently divergent that reference-based mapping fails.
evidence: Inference from missing data patterns

claim: The distribution of SNV diversity along all C. tropicalis chromosomes is extremely heterogeneous.
source: We found that the distribution of SNV diversity along all chromosomes is extremely heterogeneous in C. tropicalis.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Background diversity in C. tropicalis is the lowest among the three selfing Caenorhabditis species.
source: Background diversity in C. tropicalis (median θw) is the lowest among the three selfers
evidence: Comparison of diversity data across species shown in Figure 2A

claim: The median number of SNV differences between C. tropicalis isolates in 10 kb windows is just 3.2 on chromosome centers.
source: and the median number of SNV differences between isolates (π) in 10 kb windows is just 3.2 on chromosome centers, and less than double that on arms (genotype set 2).
evidence: Supported by diversity data

claim: Variance in diversity around the background in C. tropicalis is almost eight times that of C. elegans.
source: Variance around the background is almost eight times that of C. elegans and more than 100 times that of C. briggsae (data in Figure 2A).
evidence: Comparison of variance across species shown in Figure 2A

claim: Divergent regions cover just over 14% of the NIC58 genome.
source: and divergent regions cover just over 14% of the NIC58 genome in sum.
evidence: Supported by analysis of diversity data

claim: Genetic diversity in C. tropicalis is typified by a near-invariant background punctuated by regions of high divergence.
source: Genetic diversity in C. tropicalis is thus typified by a near-invariant background, suggesting very recent global shared ancestry, punctuated by regions of high divergence, consistent with a possible role for balancing selection.
evidence: Interpretation of diversity data with speculation about balancing selection

claim: From genome alignment between JU1373 and NIC58, there was a 37% increase in SNVs over reference-based mapping.
source: From 78.86 Mb of aligned bases (69.18 at single copy), we saw a 37% increase in SNVs over reference-based mapping
evidence: Comparison of variant calling methods

claim: SNV divergence between JU1373 and NIC58 in 10 kb windows commonly exceeded 10% on the arms.
source: SNV divergence in 10 kb windows commonly exceeded 10% on the arms (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Total divergence between JU1373 and NIC58 exceeded 30% in windows on every chromosome.
source: and total divergence (the sum of variant length differences relative to NIC58) exceeded 30% in windows on every chromosome.
evidence: Supported by analysis of genome alignment data

claim: Reference-based SNV calling dramatically underestimated the true levels of genetic diversity at divergent loci in C. tropicalis.
source: Reference-based SNV calling thus dramatically underestimated the true levels of genetic diversity at divergent loci
evidence: Comparison of reference-based and alignment-based variant calling

claim: C. tropicalis shows strong population structure, with the top principal component differentiating three African isolates from all others and accounting for almost 75% of nuclear genetic relatedness.
source: We observed strong structure, with the top axis differentiating three African isolates from all others and accounting for almost 75% of nuclear genetic relatedness (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The close clustering of three African C. tropicalis lines isolated across more than 9000 km is remarkable.
source: The close clustering of the three African lines, isolated across a transect spanning more than 9000 km from the Atlantic island of Cape Verde, off the Westernmost coast of continental Africa, to Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean, is remarkable given the large geographic distances separating these locales
evidence: Interpretation of PCA data in geographic context

claim: The second principal component differentiates Western Pacific C. tropicalis samples from all others.
source: The second principal component differentiates Western Pacific samples (Hawaii, Taiwan) from all others
evidence: Supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The first three principal components account for 89% of the genetic variance in C. tropicalis.
source: These three dimensions account for 89% of the genetic variance
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis

claim: Chromosome IV shows much more complex patterns of relatedness than the genome-wide view in C. tropicalis.
source: Notably, chromosome IV shows much more complex patterns of relatedness
evidence: Supported by chromosome-specific PCA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Chromosome V and the mitochondrial genome provide evidence of recent admixture in C. tropicalis.
source: and both chromosome V and the mitochondrial genome provide evidence of recent admixture, with strain QG834 from Panama clustering with strains from East Asia and the Pacific.
evidence: Supported by chromosome-specific PCA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Structuring of the X chromosome is particularly extreme in C. tropicalis, with essentially two haplotypes present accounting for 98% of the genetic variance.
source: Structuring of the X is particularly extreme, with essentially two haplotypes present in our sample, African and non-African, and this split accounts for 98% of the genetic variance (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by chromosome-specific PCA shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: The structure of C. tropicalis populations combines strong global differentiation, widespread homogeneity, and diversity at the very local scale.
source: The structure of C. tropicalis populations therefore combines strong, global differentiation, as seen between tropical and temperate C. briggsae clades; widespread homogeneity, as seen in C. elegans outside the Pacific; and diversity at the very local scale, common to all three selfing species (Andersen et al., 2012; Barrière and Félix, 2007; Félix et al., 2013; Haber et al., 2005; Sivasundar and Hey, 2005).
evidence: Synthesis of population structure findings with comparison to other species

claim: A locus on the center of the X chromosome explained close to 15% of the variance in hermaphrodite outcrossing probability in C. tropicalis RILs.
source: Linkage mapping detected a significant effect of a locus on the center of the X chromosome (Figure 4B), which explained close to 15% of the variance in hermaphrodite outcrossing probability.
evidence: Supported by QTL mapping data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The self-progeny of NIC58 hermaphrodites was 0.8% male versus 0.06% in JU1373.
source: The self-progeny of NIC58 hermaphrodites was 0.8% male (21/2580) versus 0.06% in JU1373 (2/3088)
evidence: Supported by counting data

claim: NIC58 and JU1373 differ heritably in male crossing ability, hermaphrodite crossing ability, equilibrium sex ratio, and spontaneous male production rate.
source: These two strains thus differ heritably in male crossing ability, hermaphrodite crossing ability, equilibrium sex ratio, and spontaneous male production rate, providing multiple paths for the evolution of outcrossing rate.
evidence: Synthesis of multiple phenotypic observations

claim: RIL genotypes revealed strong transmission ratio distortion in two genomic regions: the left arm of chromosome III and the right arm of chromosome V.
source: The RIL genotypes revealed strong transmission ratio distortion in two genomic regions: the left arm of chromosome III and the right arm of chromosome V (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RIL genotype data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Transmission ratio distortion on chromosome III reached a frequency of 97% for JU1373 homozygotes.
source: Both were strongly skewed toward JU1373 homozygotes, which reached a frequency of 97% on chromosome III
evidence: Supported by RIL genotype data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Transmission ratio distortion on chromosome V reached a frequency of 78% for JU1373 homozygotes.
source: and 78% on chromosome V.
evidence: Supported by RIL genotype data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The chromosome V locus showed an excess of heterozygotes (16% of RILs) compared to the neutral expectation after 10 generations of selfing.
source: The chromosome V locus also showed an excess of heterozygotes (16% of RILs) compared to the neutral expectation after 10 generations of selfing (1/210 = 0.1%).
evidence: Comparison of observed heterozygosity to theoretical expectation

claim: RILs that retained heterozygosity on chromosome V showed a significant enrichment of JU1373 genotypes on chromosome I.
source: RILs that retained heterozygosity on chromosome V also showed a significant enrichment of JU1373 genotypes on chromosome I (18.2–20.7 cM), which itself showed mild distortion in favor of JU1373 (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of RIL genotypes

claim: Selection during RIL construction strongly favored JU1373 alleles on chromosomes III and V.
source: These data indicate that selection during RIL construction strongly favored JU1373 alleles on chromosomes III and V
evidence: Inference from transmission ratio distortion data

claim: Complex selection at the chromosome V locus favored heterozygotes over JU1373 homozygotes under some conditions.
source: with complex selection at the locus on chromosome V favoring heterozygotes over JU1373 homozygotes under some conditions.
evidence: Inference from excess heterozygosity and genotype associations

claim: RILs homozygous for NIC58 alleles at transmission ratio distortion loci showed normal growth characteristics, with 93.1–98.3% of embryos developing into adults with parental developmental timing.
source: We examined RILs of such genotypes and found that their growth characteristics were superficially normal, with 93.1–98.3% (n = 151–679) of embryos developing into adults with parental developmental timing (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The cause of transmission ratio distortion in C. tropicalis is more complex than a simple mitochondrial-nuclear incompatibility.
source: This finding indicated that the cause of transmission ratio distortion was more complex than a simple mitochondrial-nuclear incompatibility between these NIC58 alleles and JU1373 mitochondria.
evidence: Inference from RIL viability data

claim: Far fewer F2 embryos from NIC58 × JU1373 crosses developed into adults within the normal developmental time than expected from a two-Medea model.
source: We observed that far fewer F2 embryos developed into adults within the normal developmental time than expected from the two-Medea model (41–45%, n = 329–1283, versus 98–99%, n = 1046–1093, for parental strains).
evidence: Comparison of observed F2 development to model predictions and parental controls

claim: Terminal phenotypes among abnormal F2 animals from NIC58 × JU1373 crosses included failure to hatch (9%), early larval arrest (39–41%), late larval arrest (5–9%), and abnormally small, thin adults (5%).
source: Terminal phenotypes among abnormal F2 animals included failure to hatch (9%), early larval arrest (39–41%), late larval arrest (5–9%), and abnormally small, thin adults (5%, n = 329–381)
evidence: Supported by phenotypic scoring of F2 animals

claim: F2 populations from NIC58 × JU1373 crosses experienced widespread developmental arrest at proportions higher than expected under a model of two Medea loci.
source: These data show that F2 populations experienced widespread developmental arrest, at proportions higher than expected under a model of two Medea loci.
evidence: Comparison of observed arrest to model predictions

claim: The total arrest proportion among F2 individuals reflects the effects of two Medea loci plus additional background incompatibilities.
source: One interpretation is that the total arrest proportion among F2 individuals reflects the effects of two Medea loci (<44% of F2 animals), plus additional background incompatibilities (>12–15% of F2 animals).
evidence: Interpretation of F2 arrest data

claim: Alleles at both transmission ratio distortion loci were transmitted to F2 progeny in Mendelian proportions, showing that meiosis and fertilization are not affected.
source: We observed that alleles at both loci were transmitted to progeny in Mendelian proportions, showing that meiosis and fertilization are not affected by the loci and that distortion is due to postzygotic lethality.
evidence: Supported by F2 genotype data shown in Figure 6A

claim: For the chromosome III locus, NIC58 homozygotes underwent complete developmental arrest in the mito-JU1373 cross but very little developmental arrest in the mito-NIC58 cross.
source: For the chromosome III locus, NIC58 homozygotes underwent complete developmental arrest in the mito-JU1373 cross but very little developmental arrest, compared to other genotypes, in the mito-NIC58 cross (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by F2 genotype-phenotype data shown in Figure 6A

claim: For the chromosome V locus, NIC58 homozygotes experienced highly penetrant developmental arrest in both reciprocal crosses.
source: For the chromosome V locus, NIC58 homozygotes experienced highly penetrant developmental arrest in both crosses (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by F2 genotype-phenotype data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Chromosome V JU1373 homozygotes experienced developmental arrest in both reciprocal crosses, but with lower penetrance, especially in the mito-JU1373 cross.
source: Chromosome V JU1373 homozygotes also experienced developmental arrest in both crosses, but with a lower penetrance, especially in the mito-JU1373 cross (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by F2 genotype-phenotype data shown in Figure 6A

claim: For the chromosome III locus, the JU1373 Medea allele is active in its own mitochondrial background but inactive or very weakly active in the opposite mitochondrial background.
source: for the locus on chromosome III, the Medea allele (JU1373) is active in its own mitochondrial background but inactive or very weakly active in the opposite mitochondrial background
evidence: Interpretation of F2 genotype-phenotype data

claim: For the chromosome V locus, both JU1373 and NIC58 alleles act as Medea elements and are effectively antagonistic.
source: for the locus on chromosome V, both alleles (JU1373 and NIC58) act as Medea elements and are effectively antagonistic
evidence: Interpretation of F2 genotype-phenotype data

claim: The JU1373 chromosome V Medea acts strongly in both mitochondrial backgrounds.
source: JU1373 acts strongly in both mitochondrial backgrounds
evidence: Interpretation of F2 genotype-phenotype data

claim: The NIC58 chromosome V Medea acts strongly in its own mitochondrial background and more weakly in the opposite mitochondrial background.
source: whereas NIC58 acts strongly in its own mitochondrial background and more weakly in the opposite mitochondrial background (Figure 6C).
evidence: Interpretation of F2 genotype-phenotype data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Antagonistic haplotypes at the chromosome V locus provide a simple explanation for the retention of heterozygosity at this locus among the RILs.
source: Importantly, this finding of antagonistic haplotypes at the chromosome V locus provides a simple explanation for the retention of heterozygosity at this locus among the RILs, since both classes of homozygous segregants from a hermaphrodite heterozygous for the chromosome V locus arrest (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Logical inference connecting antagonistic Medeas to observed heterozygosity

claim: JU1373 V homozygotes in a mito-NIC58 background produced progeny that were superficially wild type, with typical brood sizes and developmental rates.
source: These animals produced progeny that were superficially wild type, with typical brood sizes and developmental rates.
evidence: Supported by observation of F2 animals from specific cross shown in Figure 6B

claim: Simple mitochondrial-nuclear incompatibility is excluded as a contributor to developmental arrest of chromosome V JU1373 homozygotes.
source: This finding excludes simple mitochondrial-nuclear incompatibility as a contributor to developmental arrest of chromosome V JU1373 homozygotes.
evidence: Inference from viability of JU1373 V homozygotes in mito-NIC58 background

claim: Differences in arrest according to mitochondrial genotype reflect greater activity of the NIC58 Medea on chromosome V in a mito-NIC58 background than in a mito-JU1373 background.
source: We conclude that differences in arrest according to mitochondrial genotype reflect greater activity of the NIC58 Medea on chromosome V in a mito-NIC58 background than in a mito-JU1373 background.
evidence: Inference from genotype-phenotype data across mitochondrial backgrounds

claim: Activity of the NIC58 Medea in the mito-JU1373 background is likely dependent on additional nuclear background factors.
source: We also conclude that activity of the NIC58 Medea in the mito-JU1373 background is likely dependent on additional nuclear background factors, thus accounting for heterozygosity in the RILs being preferentially retained in certain genetic backgrounds (e.g., in animals with JU1373 alleles on the left arm of chromosome I).
evidence: Inference from association between chromosome V heterozygosity and chromosome I genotypes

claim: Lethality in C. tropicalis is not caused by simple mitochondrial × zygotic incompatibilities.
source: Thus, lethality in C. tropicalis is not caused by simple mitochondrial × zygotic incompatibilities, although two of the three Medea elements are more active in the mitochondrial background of their parental strain (Figure 6C).
evidence: Synthesis of genetic data excluding simple incompatibility model

claim: Crosses segregating only the chromosome III Medea in a mito-JU1373 background showed median rates of normal development consistent with Medea activity at a single locus (68–75%).
source: We observed that crosses segregating only the chromosome III Medea in a mito-JU1373 background showed median rates of normal development consistent with Medea activity at a single locus (68–75%, n = 218–240)
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Crosses segregating only the chromosome III Medea in a mito-NIC58 background showed no Medea activity.
source: crosses in a mito-NIC58 background showed no such activity (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The chromosome III Medea is active in the absence of segregation at the chromosome V locus.
source: These data show that the chromosome III Medea is active in the absence of segregation at the chromosome V locus
evidence: Inference from crosses with fixed chromosome V genotype

claim: The chromosome III Medea requires a mito-JU1373 genetic background.
source: and confirm that the chromosome III Medea requires a mito-JU1373 genetic background.
evidence: Inference from differential activity across mitochondrial backgrounds

claim: Crosses segregating only at the chromosome V locus showed median rates of normal development consistent with antagonistic Medea activity at a single locus (54–61% in mito-JU1373 background; 52–53% in mito-NIC58 background).
source: Crosses segregating only at the chromosome V locus showed median rates of normal development that were similar across mitochondrial backgrounds and consistent with antagonistic Medea activity at a single locus (54–61%, n = 203–321, in a mito-JU1373 background; 52–53%, n = 313–345, in a mito-NIC58 background; Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Antagonistic Medea haplotypes at the chromosome V locus act in the absence of variation at the chromosome III locus.
source: This result shows that antagonistic Medea haplotypes at the chromosome V locus act in the absence of variation at the chromosome III locus.
evidence: Inference from crosses with fixed chromosome III genotype

claim: Crosses segregating no Medeas showed median rates of normal development usually higher than 75%, but with high variability (medians ranging from 65 to 100%).
source: For comparison, crosses segregating no Medeas showed median rates of normal development that were usually higher than 75%, as expected for crosses lacking drive activity (Figure 7A); nonetheless, rates of normal development in these crosses were highly variable and sometimes low, with medians ranging from 65 to 100% (n = 163–213)
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Additional background incompatibilities are widespread and diffuse in the NIC58 × JU1373 cross.
source: suggesting a contribution from non-Medea background incompatibilities. We conclude that the chromosome III and V Medea loci act independently of one other, and that additional background incompatibilities are widespread and diffuse in the NIC58 × JU1373 cross.
evidence: Inference from variability in control crosses

claim: All three C. tropicalis Medea loci (JU1373 chromosome III, JU1373 chromosome V, and NIC58 chromosome V) act via maternal effect and not paternal effect.
source: Crosses testing the JU1373 and NIC58 Medeas showed that all acted via maternal, and not paternal, effect (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by crosses testing parental effects shown in Figure 7B

claim: The JU1373 Medea on chromosome III was mapped to an interval of around 33 kb.
source: This analysis mapped Medeas to intervals of around 33 kb on chromosome III
evidence: Supported by genetic mapping data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The JU1373 Medea on chromosome V was mapped to an interval of around 69 kb.
source: and 69 kb on chromosome V (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by genetic mapping data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: The chromosome III Medea interval encompasses a locus of locally elevated sequence divergence between NIC58 and JU1373.
source: The chromosome III interval encompasses a locus of locally elevated sequence divergence between NIC58 and JU1373, in an otherwise well-conserved region.
evidence: Supported by sequence divergence data shown in Figure 8A

claim: An insertion of sequence in JU1373 at the chromosome III Medea locus includes seven predicted genes: six are tandem duplications of neighboring genes in NIC58; the seventh is a duplication of a gene located 0.68 Mb away.
source: A clear candidate is an insertion of sequence in JU1373 that includes seven predicted genes (Figure 8A): six are tandem duplications of neighboring genes in NIC58; the seventh is a duplication of a gene located 0.68 Mb to the right in both NIC58 and JU1373.
evidence: Supported by genome annotation data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Five of the seven genes in the JU1373 chromosome III insertion have no detectable protein or nucleotide homology outside C. tropicalis.
source: Five of the seven genes have no detectable protein or nucleotide homology outside C. tropicalis.
evidence: Supported by homology analysis

claim: Two genes in the JU1373 chromosome III insertion are homologous to C. elegans genes F44E2.8 and F40F8.11, which share NADAR and YbiA-like superfamily protein domains.
source: The remaining two are homologous to C. elegans genes F44E2.8 and F40F8.11, which share NADAR and YbiA-like superfamily protein domains.
evidence: Supported by homology analysis

claim: JU1373 carries an eighth gene inserted within the original copy of the duplicated sequence at the chromosome III Medea locus, which is novel and has no detectable homology to any gene in NIC58 or in any other species.
source: In addition to these seven genes, JU1373 also carries an eighth gene inserted within the original copy of the duplicated sequence (Figure 8A, arrowhead). This gene is novel and has no detectable homology to any gene in NIC58 or in any other species.
evidence: Supported by genome annotation and homology analysis shown in Figure 8A

claim: The JU1373 Medea on chromosome III contains a total of eight additional genes compared to NIC58: one unique to JU1373, and five with no homology outside C. tropicalis.
source: Thus, the JU1373 Medea on chromosome III contains a total of eight additional genes compared to NIC58: one unique to JU1373, and five with no homology outside C. tropicalis.
evidence: Summary of gene content differences

claim: The chromosome V Medea locus lies in a region of high divergence between NIC58 and JU1373, extending well beyond the mapped interval.
source: The chromosome V locus lies in a region of high divergence between NIC58 and JU1373, extending well beyond the mapped interval (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by divergence data shown in Figure 5B

claim: A major structural difference between JU1373 and NIC58 haplotypes at the chromosome V locus is an expansion of divergent F-box-domain-encoding genes, from three homologs in NIC58 to 13 in JU1373.
source: A major structural difference between JU1373 and NIC58 haplotypes is an expansion of divergent F-box-domain-encoding genes, expanded from three homologs in NIC58 to 13 in JU1373.
evidence: Supported by genome annotation data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Immediately flanking the F-box expansion in JU1373 is a duplication of a gene encoding a homolog of the checkpoint kinase chk-2.
source: Immediately flanking this expansion in JU1373 is a duplication of a gene located 0.6 Mb away (and present in both NIC58 and JU1373), which encodes a homolog of the checkpoint kinase chk-2.
evidence: Supported by genome annotation data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Adjacent to the chk-2 homolog at the chromosome V locus is a tandem duplication of a nuclear gene encoding a mitochondrial ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase complex protein.
source: Adjacent to the chk-2 homolog is a tandem duplication of a nuclear gene encoding a mitochondrial ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase complex protein, perhaps accounting for the interaction of Medea activity with mitochondrial genotype.
evidence: Supported by genome annotation data with speculation about functional relevance

claim: The core functional complement of mitochondrial genomes is superficially identical between JU1373 and NIC58, with all 12 protein-coding, two ribosomal RNA, and 22 tRNA genes present and intact in both.
source: We also examined the mitochondrial genomes of JU1373 and NIC58, and found that the core functional complement is superficially identical; all 12 protein-coding, two ribosomal RNA, and 22 tRNA genes are called as present and intact in both (Bernt et al., 2013; Lemire, 2005; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial genome annotation

claim: There are 12 missense variants in six of the core protein coding genes between JU1373 and NIC58 mitochondrial genomes.
source: There are, however, several differences of unknown significance, including 12 missense variants in six of the core protein coding genes
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial genome comparison shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Crosses between 12 of 13 wild C. tropicalis isolates and JU1373d showed putative Medea activity.
source: We observed that crosses to JU1373d showed putative Medea activity for 12 of 13 isolates (Figure 9A)
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 9A

claim: The strength of Medea activity in crosses to JU1373d was associated with geographic origin and haplotype at the chromosome III and V Medea loci.
source: and the strength of activity was associated with geographic origin, and haplotype at the chromosome III and V Medea loci (which are themselves associated due to population structure).
evidence: Supported by comparison of developmental assay data with geographic and haplotype data shown in Figure 9

claim: The two African C. tropicalis isolates showed the least Medea activity in crosses to JU1373d and had haplotypes similar to JU1373 at both Medea loci.
source: The two African isolates showed the least activity and had haplotypes similar to JU1373 at both Medea loci
evidence: Supported by developmental assay and haplotype data shown in Figure 9

claim: Five American C. tropicalis isolates showed consistently higher Medea activity in crosses to JU1373d and carried haplotypes dissimilar to JU1373 at both Medea loci.
source: five American isolates showed consistently higher activity and carried haplotypes dissimilar to JU1373 at both Medea loci
evidence: Supported by developmental assay and haplotype data shown in Figure 9

claim: Some C. tropicalis isolates showed median rates of normal development consistent with segregation of three or more Medeas (NIC517 and QG834, 20–28%).
source: and some isolates showed median rates of normal development consistent with segregation of three or more Medeas (NIC517 and QG834, 20–28%, n = 257–276).
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 9A

claim: The JU1373 Medeas may be fixed within Africa but polymorphic or absent elsewhere.
source: This pattern suggests that the JU1373 Medeas may be fixed within Africa but polymorphic or absent elsewhere
evidence: Inference from geographic patterns of Medea activity and haplotypes

claim: Some non-African C. tropicalis isolates may contribute additional Medeas of their own.
source: and that some of the non-African isolates may contribute additional Medeas of their own.
evidence: Inference from high levels of developmental arrest in some crosses

claim: Putative Medea activity was observed in six of nine crosses between wild isolates and NIC58.
source: Among crosses to NIC58, putative Medea activity was observed in six of nine crosses (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by developmental assay data shown in Figure 9A

claim: Putative Medea activity is widespread in C. tropicalis: Medeas sometimes segregate within a geographic region, and some crosses may segregate additional elements to those identified in the NIC58 × JU1373 cross.
source: Nonetheless, these data as a whole indicate that putative Medea activity is widespread: Medeas sometimes segregate within a geographic region, and some crosses may segregate additional elements to those identified in the NIC58 × JU1373 cross.
evidence: Synthesis of Medea activity data across multiple crosses

claim: High rates of selfing can dramatically slow the rate of spread of a Medea element in simulations.
source: We found that in a large population, high rates of selfing can dramatically slow the rate of spread of a Medea element, and indeed can reduce its efficacy such that it fails to increase in frequency during 100 generations of simulated evolution (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10A

claim: In small populations, Medea elements introduced at 5% frequency are rapidly fixed under random mating but lost to drift under high rates of selfing.
source: In small populations, elements introduced at 5% frequency are rapidly fixed under random mating but lost to drift under high rates of selfing (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10B

claim: Once a Medea element is at high frequency, selfing hastens fixation of the element.
source: These simulations also reveal that once an element is at high frequency, selfing actually hastens fixation of the Medea element (compare partial selfing at S = 0.25 to obligate outcrossing at S = 0).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10A

claim: Partial selfing slows or prevents the spread of Medea elements at low frequency but hastens their fixation at high frequency.
source: These results show that partial selfing slows or prevents the spread of Medea elements at low frequency but hastens their fixation at high frequency.
evidence: Summary of simulation results

claim: Intermediate levels of selfing cause frequency-dependent selection against the rarer haplotype in simulations with antagonistic Medeas.
source: We found that intermediate levels of selfing cause frequency-dependent selection against the rarer haplotype (Figure 10C, lower panel, and Figure 10—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: Allele frequencies of antagonistic Medeas drift as though neutral under both obligate selfing and obligate outcrossing in simulations.
source: Surprisingly, allele frequencies of the antagonistic Medeas drift as though neutral under both obligate selfing and obligate outcrossing, albeit for different reasons.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: With obligate selfing, antagonistic Medea alleles are literally neutral because there are no heterozygotes.
source: With obligate selfing, there are simply no heterozygotes and the alleles are literally neutral.
evidence: Logical inference from simulation model

claim: Under obligate outcrossing, overdominance in the offspring generation is offset by underdominance in the parental generation for antagonistic Medeas, resulting in drift-like dynamics.
source: Under obligate outcrossing, overdominance generated in the offspring generation by the killing of both homozygote classes is offset by underdominance in the parental generation, because the costs of these deaths are borne by heterozygote mothers. The net effect is that the alleles exhibit drift-like dynamics despite the enormous selective cost.
evidence: Logical inference from simulation model

claim: When a strong Medea invades a population with a weaker resident Medea, the strong haplotype spreads if outcrossing rates are high but is eliminated under moderate to high rates of selfing.
source: When a strong Medea invades a population with a weaker resident Medea, the strong haplotype spreads if outcrossing rates are high but is eliminated under moderate to high rates of selfing (Figure 10—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2D,E

claim: Selfing reduces Medea load both by decreasing heterozygote frequency and by inducing strong positive frequency-dependent selection that prevents antagonistic alleles from co-occurring.
source: Overall, selfing reduces Medea load both by decreasing heterozygote frequency and by inducing strong positive frequency-dependent selection that prevents antagonistic alleles from co-occurring.
evidence: Summary of simulation results

claim: Group selection in patchy environments is sufficient to generate a global change in allele frequency for antagonistic Medeas.
source: With antagonistic Medeas, modeled with equal penetrance, the reduction in heterozygote brood size is greater and the directional effects of single-Medea genic selection are absent. In these conditions, group selection is sufficient to generate a global change in allele frequency (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 10C

claim: The joint effects of selfing and group selection on antagonistic Medeas are to eliminate the rarer allele most efficiently at intermediate selfing rates.
source: Overall, the joint effects of selfing and group selection on antagonistic Medeas are therefore to eliminate the rarer allele. Selection achieves this result most efficiently at intermediate selfing rates.
evidence: Summary of simulation results

claim: C. tropicalis is the most genetically homogeneous of the three selfing Caenorhabditis species on average.
source: our data confirm that C. tropicalis is indeed the most genetically homogeneous of the three selfers, on average
evidence: Comparison of diversity data across species

claim: The high genetic homogeneity of C. tropicalis implies a correspondingly high rate of selfing, low rate of effective recombination, and small effective population size.
source: which implies a correspondingly high rate of selfing, low rate of effective recombination, and small effective population size.
evidence: Inference from population genetic theory

claim: Three Medea gene-drive systems segregate in a single cross between C. tropicalis strains NIC58 and JU1373.
source: Within two highly divergent regions, we find some striking biology: three Medea gene-drive systems segregating in a single cross.
evidence: Summary of genetic findings

claim: Genetically similar Medea elements have been found in C. elegans.
source: Genetically similar Medea elements have also been found in C. elegans (Ben-David et al., 2017; Seidel et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-David et al., 2017 and Seidel et al., 2008

claim: Medea elements are especially common in C. tropicalis.
source: but we and others have now shown that they are especially common in C. tropicalis (Ben-David et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by data in this manuscript and citation to Ben-David et al., 2020

claim: Medea elements represent a potent and surprisingly widespread form of genetic incompatibility underlying outbreeding depression in C. tropicalis.
source: They thus represent a potent and surprisingly widespread form of genetic incompatibility underlying outbreeding depression
evidence: Synthesis of findings

claim: Medea elements are a potential cause of the high effective selfing rate in C. tropicalis.
source: and a potential cause of the species' high effective selfing rate.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and simulations

claim: A large survey of C. elegans genomes found regions of high-diversity spanning up to 20% of the reference genome.
source: Most recently, a large survey of C. elegans genomes, including 15 assembled from long-reads, found regions of high-diversity spanning up to 20% of the reference genome (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020

claim: Similar heterogeneity in genetic diversity was found in a smaller sample of C. briggsae genomes.
source: Similar heterogeneity was found in a smaller sample of C. briggsae genomes.
evidence: Reference to findings in Lee et al., 2020

claim: A promising hypothesis for hyperdivergent regions in selfing Caenorhabditis genomes is the action of balancing selection across the species' range.
source: A promising hypothesis for the presence of hyperdivergent regions in genomes is the action of balancing selection across the species' range, leading to preservation of some of the presumably abundant genetic diversity of outcrossing ancestral species.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis

claim: This balancing selection hypothesis is supported in C. elegans by the enrichment of genes encoding environmentally responsive sensory factors in divergent regions.
source: This hypothesis is supported in C. elegans by the enrichment of genes encoding environmentally responsive sensory factors, which are themselves enriched for differential expression and quantitative trait loci for response to microbes isolated from natural habitats.
evidence: Reference to findings in Lee et al., 2020

claim: The presence of multiple distinct divergent haplotypes in C. elegans argues strongly against introgression as the source of islands of divergence.
source: Alternative hypotheses include introgression, a common source of islands of divergence in other animal taxa (Hedrick, 2013), but the presence of multiple distinct divergent haplotypes in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2020) argues strongly against it.
evidence: Logical inference from data in Lee et al., 2020

claim: Most divergent regions between NIC58 and JU1373 do not carry Medea factors active independent of environment and genetic background.
source: Although Medea factors may have the potential to generate balancing selection, it is clear that most divergent regions between NIC58 and JU1373 do not carry Medea factors, or, at least, not ones that are active independent of environment and genetic background.
evidence: Inference from the limited number of Medea loci identified relative to the number of divergent regions

claim: Medea elements will reliably spread in randomly mating populations.
source: Medea elements like those we discovered in C. tropicalis will reliably spread in randomly mating populations (Wade and Beeman, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wade and Beeman, 1994 and general knowledge of gene drive

claim: In the RIL construction pedigree, two Medea haplotypes swept nearly to fixation.
source: Highly penetrant killing of homozygous larvae is an exceptionally potent selective mechanism to drive allele frequency change, and in our short RIL construction pedigree we saw two haplotypes sweep nearly to fixation.
evidence: Supported by RIL genotype data

claim: C. tropicalis shows strong geographic structure, presumably exacerbated by habitat fragmentation.
source: C. tropicalis shows strong geographic structure, presumably exacerbated by habitat fragmentation, such that encounters between Medea and sensitive haplotypes may be rare.
evidence: Supported by population structure data with speculation about causes

claim: Outcrossing rates in C. tropicalis, measured under benign laboratory conditions, are relatively low on average.
source: Upon an encounter between a hermaphrodite and a male, outcrossing rates, measured under benign laboratory conditions, are relatively low on average.
evidence: Supported by mating trial data

claim: When divergent C. tropicalis isolates cross, Medeas may be inactive due to dependence on genetic background, including mitochondrial genotype, and potentially environmental factors.
source: When divergent isolates do cross, Medeas may find themselves inactive due to dependence on genetic background, including mitochondrial genotype, and, potentially, environmental factors.
evidence: Supported by genetic data showing mitochondrial and nuclear background effects, with speculation about environmental factors

claim: C. tropicalis reproduces primarily by self-fertilization, and gene-drive elements are unable to gain traction when heterozygotes are infrequent.
source: Most importantly, C. tropicalis reproduces primarily by self-fertilization, and gene-drive elements are unable to gain traction when heterozygotes are infrequent.
evidence: Supported by mating system data and simulation results

claim: The patchy, ephemeral microhabitat of C. tropicalis provides a perfect substrate for group selection.
source: At the same time, the patchy, ephemeral microhabitat of C. tropicalis – rotting fruits and flowers on the forest floor – provides a perfect substrate for group selection.
evidence: Inference from natural history and simulation results

claim: The chromosome V Medeas occur on ancient haplotypes, evidenced by extreme divergence between NIC58 and JU1373.
source: At the same time, the chromosome V Medeas occur on ancient haplotypes, evidenced by extreme divergence between NIC58 and JU1373 (Figure 5; Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by divergence data shown in Figures 5 and 8

claim: The chromosome V haplotypes may encode unique toxin-antidote pairs that arose independently, or they may encode pairs that co-evolved from a common ancestor but are no longer cross-compatible.
source: These haplotypes may encode unique toxin-antidote pairs that arose independently, or they may encode toxin-antidote pairs that co-evolved from a common ancestor but are no longer cross-compatible.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary origins

claim: The causal genes underlying the JU1373 and NIC58 Medeas remain to be identified.
source: The causal genes underlying the JU1373 and NIC58 Medeas remain to be identified
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge

claim: The causal genes for C. tropicalis Medeas likely include one or more of the multiple genes unique to these haplotypes.
source: but likely include one or more of the multiple genes unique to these haplotypes, as seen for C. elegans where toxin and antidote functions are encoded by genes present on the killing haplotype and absent (or pseudogenized) on the non-killing haplotype (Ben-David et al., 2017; Seidel et al., 2008).
evidence: Inference from gene content differences and comparison to C. elegans

claim: A common pattern emerging from Medea systems is that maternal-effect drivers are encoded by dispensable genes with dedicated functions.
source: A common pattern emerging from these systems is that maternal-effect drivers (and the single example of a paternal-effect driver) are encoded by dispensable genes with dedicated functions, rather than genes acquiring toxin or antidote activity while retaining an ancestral non-drive function.
evidence: Synthesis of findings across multiple systems

claim: Mechanisms of translational control in the Caenorhabditis germline may make it easy for Medeas to arise.
source: A second option is that mechanisms of translational control in the Caenorhabditis germline may make it easy for Medeas to arise.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis

claim: Early embryogenesis in Caenorhabditis is largely controlled by maternal regulators.
source: Early embryogenesis in Caenorhabditis is largely controlled by maternal regulators, and a common expression pattern for these regulators is ubiquitous expression of mRNA in the oocyte but no translation until embryogenesis (Evans, 2005; Robertson and Lin, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evans, 2005 and Robertson and Lin, 2015

claim: High rates of selfing may facilitate the antidote-first scenario for Medea evolution.
source: The antidote-first scenario, in which Medeas arise from sequential mutations on a single haplotype, may be facilitated by high rates of selfing.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis

claim: In populations with high selfing rates, alternate haplotypes rarely encounter one another in heterozygotes and can evolve as though in allopatry.
source: In populations with high selfing rates, alternate haplotypes rarely encounter one another in heterozygotes. Each can then evolve as though in allopatry with the other.
evidence: Logical inference from mating system

claim: Toxin-first evolution of Medeas is possible, aided by metapopulation structure and selfing.
source: Toxin-first evolution is also possible, aided by metapopulation structure and selfing.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis

claim: Whether the toxin-antidote elements in C. tropicalis and C. elegans arose before the transition to selfing is unclear.
source: Whether the toxin-antidote elements in C. tropicalis and C. elegans arose before the transition to selfing is unclear
evidence: Statement about uncertainty

claim: The level of divergence between opposite haplotypes at Medea loci is suggestive of sampling from outcrossing ancestors.
source: although the level of divergence between opposite haplotypes at Medea loci is suggestive of sampling from outcrossing ancestors.
evidence: Inference from divergence data

claim: Unlinked modifiers affect Medea activity in C. tropicalis.
source: Our data show that unlinked modifiers affect Medea activity in C. tropicalis
evidence: Supported by genetic data showing chromosome I effects on chromosome V Medea

claim: Whether modifiers of Medea activity in C. tropicalis evolved as suppressors is equivocal.
source: though whether these modifiers evolved as suppressors is equivocal.
evidence: Statement about uncertainty in interpretation

claim: Selection for mitochondrial suppressors of maternal-effect drivers may be especially strong because mitochondria cannot segregate away from drivers via inheritance in sperm.
source: In the case of maternal-effect drivers, mitochondrial suppressors are special: selection for mitochondrial suppressors may be especially strong because mitochondria cannot segregate away from drivers via inheritance in sperm.
evidence: Logical inference from inheritance patterns

claim: The mitochondrial genotypes non-permissive for Medea drive may have evolved as suppressors, or Medeas may have arisen in permissive mitochondrial backgrounds.
source: This selective environment may explain why two of the Medeas we discovered in C. tropicalis (the chromosome III JU1373 Medea and the chromosome V NIC58 Medea) were differentially active according to mitochondrial genotype – the mitochondrial genotypes non-permissive for Medea drive may have evolved as suppressors. Alternatively, Medeas may have arisen in permissive mitochondrial backgrounds, with little selection for or against alternate mitochondrial genotypes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of mitochondrial effects

claim: The data provide little conclusive evidence that the Medea loci experience selection in nature that is due to their drive activity.
source: Ultimately, our data provide little conclusive evidence that the Medea loci experience selection in nature that is due to their drive activity.
evidence: Statement about limitations of current evidence

claim: Crosses between geographically distant C. tropicalis isolates will typically reveal multiple Medea loci.
source: The data suggest that crosses between geographically distant C. tropicalis isolates will typically reveal multiple Medea loci (Figure 9).
evidence: Inference from survey of Medea activity across isolates shown in Figure 9

claim: Segregation of multiple Medeas magnifies the cost of outcrossing and reduces the possibility of suppression by a common molecular mechanism.
source: Segregation of multiple Medeas magnifies the cost of outcrossing and reduces the possibility of suppression by a common molecular mechanism, in a manner analogous to the role of multidrug therapy in preventing the evolution of drug resistance.
evidence: Logical inference with analogy to drug resistance

claim: Organisms can adapt to gene drive by altering their population biology, increasing their rates of inbreeding and selfing.
source: In such cases, organisms can adapt by altering their population biology, increasing their rates of inbreeding and selfing (Bull, 2016; Bull et al., 2019; Drury et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bull, 2016; Bull et al., 2019; Drury et al., 2017

claim: The costs of selfing as a defense against gene drive are inbreeding depression, reduced ability to adapt to new conditions, and reduced genetic variation and niche breadth.
source: The costs of selfing as a defense against gene drive are inbreeding depression; reduced ability to adapt to new conditions; and reduced genetic variation and hence niche breadth.
evidence: General knowledge of costs of selfing

claim: Selfing Caenorhabditis are typically found in nature as totally inbred lines, consistent with having purged recessive deleterious variants in their history.
source: Selfing Caenorhabditis are typically found in nature as totally inbred lines, consistent with having purged recessive deleterious variants in their history (Anderson et al., 2010; Richaud et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2010 and Richaud et al., 2018

claim: Populations of selfing Caenorhabditis can transiently increase male frequency to achieve adaptation before returning to a primarily selfing mode of reproduction.
source: While outcrossing plays an important adaptive role in selfing Caenorhabditis (Chelo et al., 2019; Morran et al., 2009; Teotónio et al., 2006; Teotonio et al., 2012), populations can transiently increase male frequency to achieve adaptation before returning to a primarily selfing mode of reproduction (Anderson et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The preservation of genetic diversity at large numbers of ancient haplotypes by balancing selection allows selfing Caenorhabditis species to occupy a wide range of habitats despite low levels of baseline genetic variation.
source: Finally, the preservation of genetic diversity at large numbers of ancient haplotypes by balancing selection allows these species to occupy a wide range of habitats despite low levels of baseline genetic variation (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020

claim: C. tropicalis harbors abundant heritable variation in outcrossing rate, with nondisjunction, male mating propensity, and hermaphrodite mating propensity all providing avenues for genetic fine-tuning.
source: We have shown that C. tropicalis harbors abundant heritable variation in outcrossing rate, with nondisjunction, male mating propensity, and hermaphrodite mating propensity all providing avenues for genetic fine-tuning of the outcrossing rate.
evidence: Summary of findings on outcrossing variation

claim: C. tropicalis hermaphrodites are uniquely resistant to the deleterious effects of interspecific matings.
source: Ting et al., 2014 found that C. tropicalis hermaphrodites are uniquely resistant to the deleterious effects of interspecific matings
evidence: Supported by citation to Ting et al., 2014

claim: Reduced activity of sperm guidance cues in C. tropicalis hermaphrodites may promote selfing over outcrossing.
source: and they interpret their findings as evidence for reduced activity of sperm guidance cues in C. tropicalis hermaphrodites.
evidence: Interpretation from Ting et al., 2014

claim: Male longevity is reduced in C. tropicalis when male pheromone is present, creating a negative feedback that tamps down male frequencies.
source: Shi et al., 2017 showed that male longevity is reduced in C. tropicalis when male pheromone is present, creating a negative feedback that tamps down male frequencies, but not in obligately outcrossing Caenorhabditis species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2017

claim: These findings are consistent with selection favoring high selfing rates in C. tropicalis.
source: These findings are consistent with selection favoring high selfing rates in C. tropicalis.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: Selfing is often considered a factor that favors the evolution of incompatibilities and outbreeding depression.
source: Selfing is often considered a factor that favors the evolution of incompatibilities and outbreeding depression, just as the independent evolution of species or subspecies often leads to incompatibilities revealed by hybridization (Fishman and Sweigart, 2018; Maheshwari and Barbash, 2011; Presgraves, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical literature

claim: Selfing reduces the effective recombination rate, allowing unlinked loci to evolve together.
source: Selfing reduces the effective recombination rate, allowing unlinked loci to evolve together.
evidence: General knowledge of selfing effects

claim: Incompatibilities in C. tropicalis appear to mostly represent interactions between tightly linked loci acting in different individuals (mothers and offspring), rather than interactions between unlinked loci.
source: Incompatibilities in C. tropicalis appear to mostly represent interactions between tightly linked loci acting in different individuals (mothers and offspring), rather than interactions between unlinked loci
evidence: Synthesis of genetic findings

claim: Outbreeding depression in C. tropicalis is mostly not mediated by recombination.
source: thus, the resulting outbreeding depression is mostly not mediated by recombination.
evidence: Inference from the nature of Medea incompatibilities

claim: C. tropicalis can escape Medea incompatibilities and restore fitness by inbreeding.
source: C. tropicalis can escape these incompatibilities and restore fitness by inbreeding.
evidence: Logical inference from Medea genetics

claim: In C. tropicalis, incompatibility may lead to increased selfing, in contrast to the usual pattern of selfing leading to incompatibility.
source: Thus, in contrast to the usual pattern of selfing leading to incompatibility, in this species incompatibility may also lead to increased selfing.
evidence: Synthesis of findings with reversal of typical causal interpretation

claim: During RIL construction, 12.2% of lines did not survive, consistent with outbreeding depression.
source: During RIL construction, 12.2% of lines did not survive, consistent with outbreeding depression.
evidence: Supported by RIL construction data

claim: C. tropicalis is widely distributed within 25° of the Equator.
source: C. tropicalis is widely distributed within 25° of the Equator and absent outside this region (Félix, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Félix, 2020
